c-m2-circle.label: Circle: area, circumference and what scales
c-m2-circle.summary: Area grows as the square of the radius, circumference as the radius. Compare shapes before computing.

c-m2-ring.label: Rings and pathways (annulus)
c-m2-ring.summary: A ring is the outer circle minus the inner: π(R² − r²) = π(R − r)(R + r).

c-m2-sector.label: Sectors, arcs and central angles
c-m2-sector.summary: A sector is a fraction θ/360° of a circle; arc = rθ when θ is in radians.

c-m2-wheel.label: Wheels, gears and distance covered
c-m2-wheel.summary: Distance per turn is the circumference; two meshed wheels cover the same linear distance, so revolutions run inversely to diameter.

c-m2-square.label: Squares and rectangles: diagonal, area, combining
c-m2-square.summary: Diagonal d = a√2, so area = d²/2. Scaling the diagonal by k scales the area by k². Pythagoras combines or splits squares.

c-m2-triangle.label: Triangle area: Heron's formula and the special points
c-m2-triangle.summary: Heron's formula needs only the three sides. An equilateral triangle's incircle, circumcircle and area all reduce to one side length.

c-m2-quad.label: Rhombus, parallelogram, trapezium, hexagon
c-m2-quad.summary: Each quadrilateral has its own area shortcut: half the diagonal product for a rhombus, base × height for a parallelogram, half the sum of parallel sides × height for a trapezium.

c-m2-pctchange.label: Percentage change in area or perimeter
c-m2-pctchange.summary: Two independent percentage changes on length and breadth combine as (1+x/100)(1+y/100) − 1, not x+y.

c-m2-cost.label: Cost of flooring, fencing or paving
c-m2-cost.summary: Find the area first, then multiply by the rate; a path or verandah's area is the outer region minus the inner.

c-m2-polygon.label: Regular polygon: sides, diagonals and angles
c-m2-polygon.summary: A convex polygon with n sides has n(n−3)/2 diagonals.

q-m2-part.short: Part or ratio of a circle
q-m2-part.label: Part of a circle, or area ratio of similar circles
q-m2-part.summary: A fraction of a garden is cultivated; the ratio of areas of two circles; the part of a circumference in a turn.

q-m2-compare.label: Same wire: circle against square
q-m2-compare.summary: The same perimeter makes a circle or a square; compare the areas.

q-m2-ring.label: Area of a ring or a path around a circle
q-m2-ring.summary: Outer and inner radius given; area of the ring, or its ratio to the whole.

q-m2-sector.label: Sector angle, arc length and area
q-m2-sector.summary: Arc and radius give the angle or the area; two sectors of one circle are compared.

q-m2-touching.label: Circles that touch each other
q-m2-touching.summary: Three equal circles, each touching the other two: the gap between them is an equilateral triangle minus three 60° sectors.

q-m2-circlegrow.label: How much the area grows when the radius grows
q-m2-circlegrow.summary: π(r+1)² − πr² = π(2r+1): a linear equation in r, not a direct read-off.

q-m2-wheel.label: Revolutions, radius and distance covered
q-m2-wheel.summary: Distance = revolutions × circumference. Given any two, find the third.

q-m2-gear.label: Two meshed gears or wheels
q-m2-gear.summary: Meshed wheels move the same linear distance, so revolutions are inversely proportional to diameter (or radius).

q-m2-square-basic.label: Diagonal, area, perimeter of a square or rectangle
q-m2-square-basic.summary: Diagonal² = 2 × area for a square; a rectangle's sides come from its area and a given ratio.

q-m2-square-scale.label: A square scaled: diagonal or area ratio
q-m2-square-scale.summary: Scaling any linear measurement (side or diagonal) by k scales the area by k².

q-m2-combine.label: One square's area equal to the sum (or difference) of others
q-m2-combine.summary: Areas add directly (Pythagoras on the sides), even though perimeters don't.

q-m2-wire-tri.label: The same length of wire, bent into a different shape
q-m2-wire-tri.summary: The perimeter is fixed; re-bending changes only how it encloses area.

q-m2-heron.label: Triangle area from its three sides
q-m2-heron.summary: s = (a+b+c)/2, area = √(s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c)); an altitude follows from area = ½ × base × height.

q-m2-equilateral.label: Equilateral triangle: incircle, circumcircle, comparisons
q-m2-equilateral.summary: For side a: area = (√3/4)a², inradius = a/(2√3), circumradius = a/√3.

q-m2-centers.label: Centroid, medians and the incentre
q-m2-centers.summary: Three medians cut a triangle into 6 equal-area pieces; the inradius is area ÷ semi-perimeter.

q-m2-medial.label: The triangle formed by the three mid-points
q-m2-medial.summary: Joining the mid-points of a triangle's sides always makes a triangle of exactly ¼ the area.

q-m2-rhombus.label: Rhombus: diagonals, side and area
q-m2-rhombus.summary: The diagonals bisect each other at right angles, so side² = (d₁/2)² + (d₂/2)², and area = ½d₁d₂.

q-m2-hexagon.label: Area of a regular hexagon
q-m2-hexagon.summary: A regular hexagon of side a is six equilateral triangles: area = (3√3/2)a².

q-m2-parallelogram.label: Parallelogram: two sides, two heights
q-m2-parallelogram.summary: Area = side × its own corresponding height, either way round; the two heights are in inverse ratio to the sides.

q-m2-trapezium.label: Trapezium: parallel sides and height
q-m2-trapezium.summary: Area = ½ × (sum of parallel sides) × height.

q-m2-pct-area.label: Percentage change in area from two dimension changes
q-m2-pct-area.summary: Combine two percentage changes as (1 + x/100)(1 + y/100) − 1, in percent.

q-m2-pct-perimeter.label: Percentage change in perimeter from unequal side changes
q-m2-pct-perimeter.summary: When every side was equal to start with, the new perimeter is the sum of the new sides; perimeter rises by the average of the percentage changes.

q-m2-cost.label: Cost of flooring a path or verandah
q-m2-cost.summary: Outer rectangle area minus inner rectangle area, then × rate per unit area.

q-m2-polygon-diag.label: Number of diagonals of a regular polygon
q-m2-polygon-diag.summary: n(n−3)/2: every pair of vertices (nC2) minus the n sides.

formulas.text: Area = πr²     Circumference = 2πr     with π = 22/7 when the radius is a multiple of 7
Similar figures: area ratio = (ratio of lengths)²
Same perimeter P: circle area = P²/(4π), square area = P²/16
Ring = π(R² − r²) = π(R − r)(R + r)     Ring ÷ whole circle = (R² − r²) ÷ R²
formulas.note: Pathway of width w around radius r: R = r + w.

formulas.text: Sector area = (θ/360°) × πr² = ½ × arc × r     Arc = rθ (θ in radians)     180° = π rad
formulas.note: 5π/6 rad = 150°. ½ × arc × r works whatever the angle unit.

formulas.text: Three mutually touching equal circles of radius r enclose a gap equal to an equilateral triangle of side 2r minus three 60° sectors
π(r+1)² − πr² = π(2r+1): the area a ring of width 1 adds, as a linear equation in r
formulas.note: With π = 22/7 the 7 often cancels against (2r+1).

formulas.text: Distance = revolutions × circumference (= πd = 2πr)     Meshed wheels: revs₁ × d₁ = revs₂ × d₂
formulas.note: Larger wheel, fewer turns for the same distance.

formulas.text: Square: diagonal d = a√2, area = a² = d²/2     Combining squares of side a, b into one of equal total area: side = √(a²+b²)
formulas.note: Area scales as (scale factor)² even though the shape is just a square.

formulas.text: Heron's formula: s = (a+b+c)/2, area = √(s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c))     altitude on side c = 2 × area ÷ c
formulas.note: A 9-12-15 or 3-4-5-scaled triangle is right-angled: Heron's then matches ½ × leg × leg.

formulas.text: Equilateral triangle, side a: area = (√3/4)a²     inradius = a/(2√3)     circumradius = a/√3 = 2 × inradius
formulas.note: Square and equilateral triangle on the same base: area ratio = 4 : √3.

formulas.text: Medians: the centroid splits each median 2:1, and the three medians cut the triangle into 6 equal-area pieces
formulas.note: A quadrilateral made of two of those pieces has twice one piece's area.

formulas.text: Joining the mid-points of a triangle's three sides gives a triangle of exactly 1/4 the original area
formulas.note: True for every triangle, not just special ones.

formulas.text: Rhombus: side² = (d₁/2)² + (d₂/2)², area = ½d₁d₂     Regular hexagon: area = (3√3/2)a²     Parallelogram: area = base × its height     Trapezium: area = ½(a+b)h
formulas.note: A parallelogram's two heights are in the inverse ratio of its two side lengths.

formulas.text: Two independent percentage changes x% and y% on length and breadth: new area is (1+x/100)(1+y/100) of the old, i.e. a net change of x + y + xy/100 percent
formulas.note: x and y carry their own sign: a decrease is negative.

formulas.text: If every side of an equilateral triangle is increased by a different percentage, the new perimeter is the sum of the new sides, so the percentage increase in perimeter is the plain average of the three percentage increases
formulas.note: (20+30+50)/3 = 33⅓%, because all three original sides were equal.

formulas.text: Path/verandah area = (outer length × outer breadth) − (inner length × inner breadth)     Cost = area × rate
formulas.note: Outer dimensions add the path's width on both sides: L+2w, B+2w.

formulas.text: Diagonals of a convex n-gon = n(n−3)/2
formulas.note: Total pairs of vertices nC2 = n(n−1)/2, minus the n sides themselves.

q-m2-part.cue: 'A garden, 80% cultivated…', 'two similar circles with radii in the ratio…', 'ratio of areas is 4:7, find ratio of radii', 'percentage of circumference in a half turn'.
q-m2-part.standard: Find the whole (πr²) and take the fraction asked: 20% of 22/7 × 28 × 28 = 492.8 cm². For ratios use the radius ratio squared, or its square root to go backwards.
q-m2-part.fast: 22/7 × 28 × 28 = 22 × 4 × 28 = 2,464; 20% of it = 492.8. For a half turn the answer is 50% whatever the radius. Going from an area ratio to a radius ratio, just take the square root.
q-m2-part.eliminate: Ask what is being asked: 'uncultivated' is the small part (20%), so the answer is a fifth of the area, and the radius cancels in a half-turn question.
traps: Taking the cultivated 80% instead of the remaining 20%.
Giving the radius ratio (5 : 8) instead of the area ratio.
Spending time on the radius when only the fraction matters.

q-m2-compare.cue: 'The same length of wire is used for a circle or a square. Ratio of the areas?' or 'the area enclosed by a wire bent into X, compare with Y'.
q-m2-compare.standard: Perimeter 80 m: square side 20, area 400. Circle: 2πr = 80, r = 40/π, area = πr² = 1,600/π ≈ 509.3. Ratio ≈ 1.27 : 1. If instead the SAME area is given for one shape, find its perimeter first, then re-use that perimeter for the other.
q-m2-compare.fast: The ratio is 4/π whatever the wire length: 4 ÷ 3.14 = 1.27.
q-m2-compare.eliminate: A circle always holds more area than a square with the same perimeter, so the ratio is above 1 (removes 1 : 1). And 4/π is a little over 1.27.
traps: Assuming equal perimeter means equal area.
Using the diameter as the radius.
Using π = 3 and getting 1.33.

q-m2-ring.cue: A circular garden with a pathway of width w around it; an annular region with outer and inner radii.
q-m2-ring.standard: Ring = π(R² − r²). Path around r = 18 with w = 2.5: R = 20.5, area = 22/7 × (20.5² − 18²) = 22/7 × 96.25 = 302.5 m². Ratio of ring to outer circle for R = 12, r = 8: (144 − 64)/144 = 5/9.
q-m2-ring.eliminate: The strip is about width × circumference at the middle: 2.5 × 2π × 19.25 ≈ 302. A strip of 2.5 around 18 is a bit more than 2.5 × 2π × 18 = 282.7.
traps: Using width × inner circumference (282.7).
Using R = r + 2w when the path is only on the outside once.
Giving the radius ratio 8 : 12 = 2 : 3 as the area ratio.

q-m2-sector.cue: 'Central angle of a sector with arc … and radius …', 'area of a sector formed by an arc of length …', or two sectors with angles in different units.
q-m2-sector.standard: Angle in radians = arc ÷ radius = 12 ÷ 4 = 3. Area = ½ × arc × radius = ½ × 3.5 × 5 = 8.75 cm². For sectors of one circle compare angles in the same unit: 5π/6 rad = 150°, so the ratio is 1 : 1.
q-m2-sector.fast: Area never needs the angle separately: it's just half the arc times the radius, the same shortcut as a triangle's ½ base × height.
q-m2-sector.eliminate: Convert units before comparing: if the two angles look different (150° and 5π/6) they may be equal.
traps: Comparing 150 with 5π/6 as raw numbers.
Dividing arc by diameter.
Finding the angle first and then re-deriving the area the long way.

q-m2-touching.cue: 'Three circles of radius r, each touching the other two. Area of the region enclosed by the three circles.'
q-m2-touching.standard: The three centres form an equilateral triangle of side 2r. Gap = (√3/4)(2r)² − 3 sectors of 60° = √3 r² − (π/2)r² = r²(√3 − π/2). For r = 3.5: 12.25 × (1.732 − 1.571) ≈ 1.975 cm².
q-m2-touching.fast: The gap is always r² × (√3 − π/2) ≈ 0.161 r² — a small sliver compared to even one circle.
q-m2-touching.eliminate: The gap must be much smaller than any one circle's area (38.5 cm² here), which rules out any option in the double digits.
traps: Giving a value close to one full circle's area.
Subtracting only one sector instead of three.
Rounding so early that the result lands on a wrong but close-looking option.

q-m2-circlegrow.cue: 'The area of a circle increases by … when its radius increases by 1. Find the original radius.'
q-m2-circlegrow.standard: π(r+1)² − πr² = π(2r+1) = the given increase. Solve the resulting linear equation for r.
q-m2-circlegrow.fast: With π = 22/7, pick an r that makes (2r+1) a multiple of 7 so the fraction cancels cleanly.
q-m2-circlegrow.eliminate: The increase grows roughly linearly with r, so a small stated increase (22 cm² here) rules out any option much above or below single digits.
traps: Solving π(r+1)² = given increase (dropping the −πr² term).
Using diameter instead of radius.
Treating the increase as proportional to r² instead of (2r+1).

q-m2-wheel.cue: 'The radius/diameter of a wheel is …. How many revolutions to cover … km/m?' or 'the wheel turns … times a minute, how long to cover …?'
q-m2-wheel.standard: Circumference = 2πr (or πd). Revolutions = total distance ÷ circumference; if a rate (revs/min) is given, time = revolutions ÷ rate.
q-m2-wheel.fast: Convert everything to the same unit first (cm or m), and look for the 22/7 to cancel against a multiple of 7 in the radius.
q-m2-wheel.eliminate: A bigger wheel needs fewer revolutions for the same distance — check the direction of any ratio before computing.
traps: Using diameter where radius was needed, or the reverse.
Forgetting to convert km to the same unit as the radius.
Dividing distance by radius instead of by circumference.

q-m2-gear.cue: 'A gear/wheel of diameter … is turning a gear of diameter …. When the smaller makes N revolutions, how many does the larger make?'
q-m2-gear.standard: Meshed wheels cover equal linear distance, so revs × diameter is the same for both: revs₂ = revs₁ × d₁/d₂.
q-m2-gear.fast: The ratio of revolutions is just the inverse ratio of the diameters (or radii) — no circumference arithmetic needed.
q-m2-gear.eliminate: The larger wheel always turns fewer times, so the answer must be less than the smaller wheel's revolution count.
traps: Multiplying by d₂/d₁ instead of d₁/d₂ (inverting the ratio).
Using radius for one wheel and diameter for the other.
Assuming equal revolutions because they're 'meshed'.

q-m2-square-basic.cue: 'The diagonal of a square is …, find its area', or 'the breadth is a fraction of the length, area given, find the difference'.
q-m2-square-basic.standard: Area = diagonal²/2. For a rectangle with breadth = k × length and area A: length² = A/k, then compute the difference.
q-m2-square-basic.fast: Square the diagonal and halve it — no need to find the side first.
q-m2-square-basic.eliminate: The area must be a little less than diagonal² (since diagonal² = 2 × area), which rules out any option close to or above the diagonal squared.
traps: Using diagonal² directly as the area (forgetting the ÷2).
Treating the breadth fraction as the ratio of sides the wrong way round.
Giving the side length where the difference of sides was asked.

q-m2-square-scale.cue: 'The diagonal of a square is …; another square has double/triple the area — find its diagonal', or 'two squares' diagonals are in the ratio …, find their area ratio'.
q-m2-square-scale.standard: Area ratio = (diagonal ratio)², so area ratio k means diagonal ratio √k. Going the other way, square the diagonal ratio to get the area ratio.
q-m2-square-scale.fast: Double the area means the diagonal scales by √2; this makes a new diagonal of 4√2 × √2 = 8 instantly, no area arithmetic needed.
q-m2-square-scale.eliminate: A diagonal ratio of 3:7 squares to 9:49, not 3:7 itself — the area ratio always looks bigger in the numerator and much bigger in the denominator once squared.
traps: Doubling the diagonal instead of scaling it by √2 for double the area.
Giving the area ratio where the diagonal ratio was asked, or the reverse.
Leaving a surd un-simplified so it doesn't match the printed option.

q-m2-combine.cue: 'The perimeters of two squares are … and …. Find the perimeter of a third square with area equal to the sum of their areas.'
q-m2-combine.standard: Perimeter → side (÷4) → area (side²) for each square; add the areas; take the square root for the new side; ×4 for the new perimeter.
q-m2-combine.fast: If the two sides are a Pythagorean-triple-like pair (6 and 8, for instance), the new side is the familiar hypotenuse (10) — recognise it instead of computing.
q-m2-combine.eliminate: The new square's side must be bigger than either original side but less than their sum — narrows the answer fast.
traps: Adding the perimeters or the sides directly instead of the areas.
Forgetting to take the square root before multiplying by 4 again.
Mixing up which square is being asked for (sum vs. difference of areas).

q-m2-wire-tri.cue: 'A string/wire of length … is bent first into a square, then (keeping one side fixed) into a right-angled triangle. Find the area of the triangle.'
q-m2-wire-tri.standard: Total length is fixed throughout. Square: side = length/4. Triangle: that side is one leg (or the base); the remaining length splits between the other two sides of a right triangle — solve a²+b²=(sum−a)² or recognise the triple.
q-m2-wire-tri.fast: Once one leg is fixed, look for a familiar Pythagorean triple among the remaining length's possible splits (6-8-10 is common).
q-m2-wire-tri.eliminate: The remaining two sides must sum to (total length − fixed side) and satisfy Pythagoras — only one split usually gives whole numbers.
traps: Assuming the triangle is equilateral or isosceles instead of right-angled as stated.
Re-using the square's area instead of recomputing the triangle's.
Splitting the remaining length evenly instead of solving for the right-angle condition.

q-m2-heron.cue: 'The sides of a triangle are …, …, … cm. Find its area' or 'find the altitude to the side measuring …'.
q-m2-heron.standard: s = (a+b+c)/2, area = √(s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c)). For the altitude on a given side: altitude = 2 × area ÷ that side.
q-m2-heron.fast: Check for a right triangle first (does a² + b² = c², or a scaled 3-4-5?) — then area is just ½ × leg × leg, no Heron's needed.
q-m2-heron.eliminate: The area must be less than ½ × (two largest sides) and more than a reasonably small fraction of the full triangle — rules out options that are far too big or too small.
traps: Using the wrong side as the base for the altitude.
Miscomputing s or one of the (s−side) factors.
Not noticing the triangle is right-angled, leading to unnecessary Heron's arithmetic that introduces errors.

q-m2-equilateral.cue: 'Equilateral triangle of side …; find the area of its incircle/circumcircle', 'compare a square and equilateral triangle on the same base', or 'circumcircle's area is …, find the triangle's perimeter'.
q-m2-equilateral.standard: Area = (√3/4)a², inradius = a/(2√3), circumradius = a/√3. Any one of {side, area, inradius, circumradius} gives all the others.
q-m2-equilateral.fast: Circumradius is always exactly twice the inradius for an equilateral triangle — a quick cross-check.
q-m2-equilateral.eliminate: The circumcircle is always bigger than the incircle (exactly 4× the area), so an option showing them equal or the incircle bigger is wrong.
traps: Using the general triangle's inradius formula (area ÷ semi-perimeter) when the direct a/(2√3) shortcut is faster.
Mixing up inradius and circumradius.
Forgetting the √3 when going from circumradius back to the side.

q-m2-centers.cue: 'O is the centroid, AD/BE/CF are the medians, area of one small triangle given, find a quadrilateral's area', 'side BC trisected at D and E, find AD', or 'inradius of a triangle with sides …'.
q-m2-centers.standard: The three medians always split the triangle into 6 equal-area pieces; any region made of a known number of those pieces follows directly. For a cevian to a trisection point, use the Apollonius-style law of cosines with the known 60° (equilateral) or given angle.
q-m2-centers.fast: Spot how many of the 6 equal pieces the asked region covers — a quadrilateral like BDOF is exactly 2 of them.
q-m2-centers.eliminate: Any area answer must be a whole multiple of the one given small-triangle area (since all 6 pieces are equal).
traps: Assuming the quadrilateral is 3 pieces instead of 2 (or vice versa).
Using the centroid's 2:1 split where the 6-equal-areas fact was the quicker route.
Dropping the cos 60° = ½ term when applying the law of cosines to a trisected side.

q-m2-medial.cue: 'The triangle formed by joining the mid-points of triangle … (sides a, b, c). Find its area.'
q-m2-medial.standard: Find the original triangle's area (Heron's, or ½ × legs if right-angled), then take exactly ¼ of it.
q-m2-medial.fast: No need to find the medial triangle's own side lengths — the ¼ rule applies regardless of the triangle's shape.
q-m2-medial.eliminate: The answer must be exactly a quarter of a 'nice' number if the original sides give a clean area (e.g. a 3-4-5 triangle has area 6, so the medial triangle is 1.5).
traps: Computing the medial triangle's own sides (half of each original side) and then re-deriving its area the long way, risking arithmetic slips.
Using half the area instead of a quarter.
Not recognising a scaled 3-4-5 right triangle, leading to unnecessary Heron's work.

q-m2-rhombus.cue: 'The diagonals of a rhombus are … and …. Find its perimeter/area', or 'one side is … and one diagonal is …, find the area'.
q-m2-rhombus.standard: Half-diagonals are legs of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is the side. Area = ½d₁d₂; perimeter = 4 × side.
q-m2-rhombus.fast: Half each diagonal and look for a Pythagorean triple (16,12,20 or 15,20,25) to get the side without a square root.
q-m2-rhombus.eliminate: The side must be longer than either half-diagonal alone, so rule out any option smaller than half the longer diagonal.
traps: Using the full diagonals as the right-triangle legs instead of halving them first.
Confusing area (½d₁d₂) with perimeter.
Taking the wrong half-diagonal as the one paired with the given side.

q-m2-hexagon.cue: 'A regular hexagon of side … cm. Find its area.'
q-m2-hexagon.standard: Area = (3√3/2) × side². Just substitute the side and simplify the surd.
q-m2-hexagon.fast: Six equilateral triangles of the same side: 6 × (√3/4)a² simplifies straight to (3√3/2)a².
q-m2-hexagon.eliminate: The answer should be a clean multiple of √3 when the side itself involves √3 (as here, side = 2√3 makes side² = 12, a whole number).
traps: Using the square's or a generic polygon's area formula instead of the hexagon-specific one.
Forgetting to square the side before multiplying by 3√3/2.
Mis-simplifying the surd when the side itself contains a √3.

q-m2-parallelogram.cue: 'Two adjacent sides of a parallelogram are … and …. If the distance between the two smaller/larger sides is …, find the other distance.'
q-m2-parallelogram.standard: Area = (one pair of sides) × (its own corresponding height) = (other pair) × (its height). Find the area from the given side-height pair, then divide by the other side to get its height.
q-m2-parallelogram.fast: The two heights are in the exact inverse ratio of the two sides — no need to compute the area as an intermediate step if only the ratio is wanted.
q-m2-parallelogram.eliminate: The height corresponding to the LONGER side must be the SMALLER of the two heights (since side × height = area is fixed) — rules out any option bigger than the given height.
traps: Pairing the given height with the wrong side (the distance between the sides of length X is the height when X is the base, not when the OTHER side is the base).
Treating the parallelogram as a rectangle.
Swapping which pair is 'smaller' vs 'bigger'.

q-m2-trapezium.cue: 'A trapezium has parallel sides … and … and height …. Find its area', or 'area and height given with a ratio of the parallel sides — find the longer one'.
q-m2-trapezium.standard: Area = ½ × (sum of parallel sides) × height. When the ratio of the two parallel sides is given instead of their values, write them as kx and write the area equation to solve for x.
q-m2-trapezium.fast: Half the height times the sum of the parallel sides — compute the sum first so there's only one multiplication left.
q-m2-trapezium.eliminate: The longer parallel side must be bigger than (2 × area ÷ height) ÷ 2 if the two sides were equal — a quick sanity bound.
traps: Forgetting the ½ in the area formula.
Using the ratio parts directly as the side lengths instead of scaling by x.
Mixing up which of the two parallel sides is being asked for.

q-m2-pct-area.cue: 'Length increased by x%, breadth increased/decreased by y%, find the % change in area', or a single shape where every side changes by the same %.
q-m2-pct-area.standard: New area ÷ old = (1+x/100)(1+y/100). Expand or multiply directly, then convert the result back to a percentage change.
q-m2-pct-area.fast: Net % change = x + y + xy/100 — just plug in the two percentages (with their signs) into this one line.
q-m2-pct-area.eliminate: If x and y have opposite signs and are numerically close, the net change is small — rules out large-magnitude options immediately.
traps: Simply adding x + y and forgetting the cross-term xy/100.
Dropping the sign on a decrease.
Applying the single-dimension-squared rule when the two changes are actually different percentages.

q-m2-pct-perimeter.cue: 'The sides of an equilateral triangle are increased by x%, y%, z% respectively to form a new triangle — find the % increase in perimeter.'
q-m2-pct-perimeter.standard: Since all three original sides were equal (say a), the new perimeter is a(1+x/100) + a(1+y/100) + a(1+z/100) = a(3 + (x+y+z)/100). Compare to the old perimeter 3a.
q-m2-pct-perimeter.fast: The % increase in perimeter is simply the average of the three given percentages: (x+y+z)/3.
q-m2-pct-perimeter.eliminate: The answer must lie between the smallest and largest of the three given percentages (it's their average).
traps: Adding the three percentages without dividing by 3.
Treating it as a percentage-change-in-AREA question (squaring something) when only the perimeter is asked.
Assuming the new triangle is still equilateral.

q-m2-cost.cue: 'A hall/garden … is surrounded by a path/verandah of width …. Find the cost of flooring it at ₹… per sq. m.'
q-m2-cost.standard: Outer rectangle = (L+2w) × (B+2w); inner = L × B; path area = outer − inner; cost = path area × rate.
q-m2-cost.fast: Expand (L+2w)(B+2w) − LB = 2w(L+B) + 4w² — a direct formula for the path's area without computing two full rectangles.
q-m2-cost.eliminate: The path area must be noticeably smaller than the full outer rectangle's area — rules out any cost close to (outer area × rate).
traps: Adding the width only once per side instead of to both length and breadth.
Computing the inner rectangle's cost instead of the path's.
Using the path's width as if it were a radius (circular-ring formula) on a rectangular path.

q-m2-polygon-diag.cue: 'If a regular polygon has n sides, how many diagonals does it have?'
q-m2-polygon-diag.fast: Total vertex pairs nC2 minus the n sides themselves — both are quick mental steps for small n.
q-m2-polygon-diag.eliminate: The count must be less than nC2 = n(n−1)/2 (that includes the sides too) — rules out any option at or above that bound.
traps: Using n(n-1)/2 (all pairs) and forgetting to subtract the n sides.
Using n(n-2)/2 (a different, unrelated formula) by mistake.
Off-by-one errors in n for a 'regular polygon with n sides' vs 'n vertices' phrasing (they're the same n, but it's easy to second-guess).
